decks.title: Morphology of Root, Stem and Leaf — Part 1: Roots and stems
goals: Distinguish tap, fibrous and adventitious roots and describe the regions of a root tip
Identify root modifications for storage, respiration and support
Classify the modifications of the stem and explain why a potato is a stem and a sweet potato a root

slides.heading: Morphology of root, stem and leaf
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the organs below the soil and the axis that bears the leaves.

visual.alt: Flow from seed to the root system from the radicle and the shoot system from the plumule

slides.narration: Morphology is the study of external form. A flowering plant has a root system that develops from the radicle of the seed, and a shoot system, from the plumule, made of the stem, branches and leaves. Both systems show many modifications that suit particular jobs.

slides.heading: Tap, fibrous and adventitious roots
slides.body_md: A **tap root** is the radicle growing on; a **fibrous root** system replaces the radicle with many thin roots; **adventitious** roots arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle.

rows: Radicle persists as main root with lateral branches
Radicle is short-lived; many roots from the base of the stem
From stem, leaf or other parts
Banyan prop roots, grass, Bryophyllum leaf

visual.alt: Table of tap, fibrous and adventitious roots with their origin, occurrence and examples

slides.narration: Dicot plants usually keep the main root, the tap root, with branches. In monocots the primary root soon dies and a mat of fibrous roots grows from the base of the stem. Adventitious roots come from other parts, such as the lower nodes of a stem.

slides.heading: Regions of a root tip
slides.body_md: From the tip upward: **root cap**, region of **meristematic activity**, region of **elongation**, and region of **maturation** with **root hairs**.

slides.narration: The root cap protects the delicate tip as it pushes through the soil. Cells just behind it divide rapidly. Further back they lengthen, which pushes the tip forward. In the oldest region the cells mature and some form root hairs that absorb water and minerals.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a root tip
slides.body_md: A young root is 40 millimetres long. The cap is 1 millimetre, the meristematic region 2 millimetres and the elongation region 6 millimetres. Find the length of the maturation region, the share taken by elongation, and the growth in a week at 3 millimetres a day.
bullets: Maturation region: 40 − 1 − 2 − 6 = **31** millimetres.
Elongation share: 6 ÷ 40 × 100 = **15 percent**.
Growth in a week: 3 × 7 = **21** millimetres.

visual.alt: Worked table of the lengths of the regions of the root tip

slides.narration: Subtract the three growing regions from the total to get the length of the maturation region. Elongation is only a small share of the root, yet it is where the root gains most of its length. Multiply the daily growth by seven to get the weekly growth.

slides.heading: Quick check: root regions
slides.body_md: In which region of the root do root hairs appear?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think of where water is absorbed.

slides.heading: The stem: nodes, internodes and buds
slides.body_md: A stem has **nodes** that bear leaves and buds, **internodes** between them, and a **terminal bud** at the tip; each leaf has an **axillary bud** in its axil.

visual.alt: Table comparing a stem with a root

slides.narration: These features tell a stem from a root. A stem has nodes where leaves or scale leaves arise, and buds in the axils. A root has none of these, but it has a cap at the tip. This is the key to the potato and the sweet potato puzzle.

slides.heading: Modified stems
slides.body_md: **Underground:** tuber, rhizome, corm. **Sub-aerial:** runner, sucker, stolon, offset. **Aerial:** tendril, thorn, phylloclade.

slides.heading: Stem modifications compared
slides.body_md: Position, example and function.

visual.alt: Table of stem modifications with position, example and function

slides.narration: Underground stems store food and carry the plant through unfavourable seasons. Sub-aerial stems run along or just under the soil and spread the plant. Aerial stems may climb, protect or photosynthesise, as in the green flattened stem of Opuntia.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: stem or root?
slides.body_md: A potato has small depressions that sprout shoots; a sweet potato has none. Count: 5 potatoes with 8 eyes each, and a grass runner 300 centimetres long with a node every 12 centimetres.
bullets: The potato has **eyes**, which are axillary buds on nodes, so it is a **stem tuber**.
The sweet potato has no nodes, internodes or buds and can form adventitious shoots only, so it is a **tuberous root**.
Eyes on 5 potatoes: 5 × 8 = **40**; nodes on the runner: 300 ÷ 12 = **25**.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing a potato and a sweet potato

slides.narration: Look for nodes and buds. The eyes of a potato are buds on nodes, so it is a stem. A sweet potato has none, so it is a root. Counts follow by multiplication and division, such as eight eyes on each of five potatoes.

slides.heading: Quick check: runner
slides.body_md: How many nodes does a 300 cm runner have if there is a node every 12 cm?
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the length by the spacing.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Roots: tap, fibrous, adventitious; the tip has a cap, meristematic, elongation and maturation regions.
Modified roots: fusiform, conical, napiform, tuberous (storage); pneumatophores (respiration); prop and stilt (support).
Stem: nodes, internodes, terminal and axillary buds.
Underground stems: tuber, rhizome, corm; sub-aerial: runner, stolon, sucker, offset; aerial: tendril, thorn, phylloclade.
A potato is a stem (eyes are buds); a sweet potato is a root.

visual.alt: Summary table of four plants, the modified organ and the modification

slides.narration: To recap: roots are tap, fibrous or adventitious, and may be modified for storage, support or respiration. Stems have nodes and buds, and may be modified underground, above ground or just at the surface. Use nodes and buds to decide stem or root.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give the **function** with every modification you name.
Say **why**: the potato is a stem because it has **eyes (buds) on nodes**.
Name the four regions of a root tip **from the tip upward**.
Label diagrams of modified roots and stems with the **plant name** as well as the type.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Always give the function of a modification. Justify with nodes and buds when a question asks whether an organ is a stem or a root. Name the root regions from the tip upward. And write the plant name on each diagram.

slides.heading: The leaf
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the organ of photosynthesis and its many forms.

visual.alt: Flow of the three parts of a typical leaf from base to lamina

slides.narration: A leaf arises at a node and has an axillary bud in its axil. A typical leaf has three parts: the leaf base, the petiole and the lamina. Leaves differ in venation, in being simple or compound, and in how they are arranged on the stem.

slides.heading: Parts of a simple leaf
slides.body_md: The **leaf base** attaches to the stem and may bear **stipules**; the **petiole** holds the **lamina** to the light; the lamina has a **midrib** and **veins**.

slides.narration: In reticulate venation the veins form a network. In parallel venation they run side by side. In a simple leaf the blade is whole. In a compound leaf the blade is cut into leaflets, borne on a rachis in a pinnate leaf and all from one point in a palmate leaf.

slides.heading: Compound leaf or branch?
slides.body_md: A compound leaf and a branch bearing simple leaves can look alike. The **bud** tells them apart.

rows: Bud in the axil of the main axis
Present at the base of the petiole
Present in the axil of the branch
Bud at the tip of the main axis
Buds in the axils of leaflets or leaves
On a rachis in one plane
On nodes, often in a spiral

visual.alt: Table distinguishing a compound leaf from a branch bearing simple leaves

slides.narration: Look for buds. A compound leaf has an axillary bud only at the base of its petiole, and no bud at the tip. A branch has a terminal bud and an axillary bud in the axil of every leaf.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting leaflets
slides.body_md: Count the leaflets: (a) a neem leaf with 9 pairs and no terminal leaflet; (b) a rose leaf with 3 pairs and a terminal leaflet; (c) a twig with 6 palmate leaves of 5 leaflets each.
bullets: Palmate twig: 6 × 5 = **30**.

visual.alt: Worked table of leaflet counts for three leaves

slides.narration: In a pinnate leaf the leaflets are in pairs along the rachis, so double the number of pairs. If there is also a terminal leaflet, add one. For palmate leaves, multiply the number of leaves by the leaflets in each leaf.

notes.title: Morphology of Root, Stem and Leaf — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The root
sections.body_md:
**Morphology** is the study of the external form of an organism. In a flowering plant the **root system** develops from the **radicle** of the embryo and the **shoot system** from the **plumule**.

**Types of root systems.** A **tap root system** has the primary root (the radicle's continuation) with its lateral branches, as in mustard and gram (dicots). A **fibrous root system** has many thin roots that arise from the base of the stem after the primary root dies, as in wheat and rice (monocots). **Adventitious roots** arise from parts of the plant other than the radicle, such as the stem or a leaf (the roots of grass, the prop roots of banyan, the roots from the leaf of *Bryophyllum*).

**Regions of a young root (from the tip).** (1) The **root cap**, a thimble-like covering that protects the tip. (2) The **region of meristematic activity**, where cells divide. (3) The **region of elongation**, where cells lengthen and the root grows in length. (4) The **region of maturation**, where cells differentiate; some epidermal cells form **root hairs**, which absorb water and minerals.

**Modifications of roots.**
- *Storage:* **fusiform** (radish), **conical** (carrot), **napiform** (turnip, beetroot), **tuberous** (sweet potato, without a definite shape).
- *Respiration:* **pneumatophores**, upright breathing roots of plants of swampy, tidal soil such as mangroves (*Rhizophora*, *Avicennia*), with pores for gas exchange.
- *Support:* **prop roots** from branches of the banyan; **stilt roots** from the lower nodes of maize, sugarcane and *Pandanus*.

*Where books differ.* Some books list five storage types and treat beet as conical or napiform; the chapter follows the syllabus examples: carrot conical, radish fusiform, turnip napiform and sweet potato tuberous.

sections.heading: 2. The stem
sections.body_md:
The stem develops from the **plumule** and bears **nodes** (where leaves arise), **internodes** between them, a **terminal bud** at the tip and an **axillary bud** in the axil of each leaf. Young stems are green; the stem has no root cap.

**Modifications of the stem**
- **Underground** (for storage and perennation): **tuber** (potato: a swollen stem whose **eyes** are axillary buds on nodes); **rhizome** (ginger, turmeric: horizontal, with nodes, scale leaves and buds); **corm** (colocasia, *Crocus*: a short, thick, vertical stem with scale leaves).
- **Sub-aerial** (propagation): **runner** (grass: creeps and roots at nodes), **stolon** (strawberry, jasmine: an arching branch that touches the soil), **sucker** (mint, chrysanthemum: a lateral branch from an underground node that grows upward), **offset** (water hyacinth, *Pistia*: a short, thick branch in aquatic plants).
- **Aerial:** **tendril** (grapevine, *Passiflora*: climbing), **thorn** (*Citrus*, *Bougainvillea*: a stem from an axillary bud, protection), **phylloclade** (*Opuntia*: a green, flattened stem that photosynthesises and stores water).

**Why a potato is a stem and a sweet potato a root.** A potato has nodes (scale leaves), internodes and axillary buds, the **eyes**, that sprout into shoots. A sweet potato has no nodes, internodes or buds, and cannot form shoots from regular buds; it is a tuberous root.

*Where books differ.* Some books place the bulb (onion) among stem modifications; ISC places the **fleshy bulb leaves** in the leaf modifications and so does this chapter, noting that the bulb is a short stem with scale leaves.

sections.heading: 3. The leaf: parts, venation, simple and compound leaves, phyllotaxy
sections.body_md:
A leaf arises at a node and has an axillary bud in its axil. A typical leaf has three parts: the **leaf base**, which may bear two lateral outgrowths, the **stipules** (dicots), or form a **sheath** round the stem (monocots; a swollen **pulvinus** in leguminous plants); the **petiole**, which holds the blade to the light; and the **lamina** (leaf blade), with a central **midrib** and **veins**.

**Venation** is the arrangement of veins: **reticulate** (a network; dicots) and **parallel** (veins side by side; monocots).

**Simple and compound leaves.** In a **simple leaf** the lamina is entire (or incised, but not cut to the midrib). In a **compound leaf** it is cut into **leaflets**. In a **pinnate** compound leaf the leaflets are on a common axis, the **rachis** (neem; rose); in a **palmate** compound leaf they all arise from the tip of the petiole (silk cotton). The **axillary bud** is present in the axil of a compound leaf (at the base of its petiole) but not in the axils of its leaflets, and there is no terminal bud on the rachis; a **branch** has a terminal bud and a bud in the axil of every leaf.

**Phyllotaxy** is the arrangement of leaves on a stem: **alternate** (one leaf at each node: China rose, mustard, sunflower), **opposite** (two leaves at each node: *Calotropis*, guava) and **whorled** (more than two leaves at each node: *Alstonia*).

sections.heading: 4. Leaf modifications and insectivorous plants
sections.body_md:
Leaves are modified for functions other than photosynthesis:
- **Support:** leaves or leaflets become **tendrils**, as in the pea.
- **Protection:** leaves become **spines**, as in *Opuntia* (the flat green phylloclade carries on photosynthesis) and in some plants that reduce water loss.
- **Storage:** **fleshy scale leaves** of the **bulb** of onion and garlic (and succulent leaves of *Aloe*) store food and water.
- **Reproduction:** in *Bryophyllum* **adventitious buds** form in the notches of the leaf margin and grow into new plants.
- **Insect trapping:** leaves of **insectivorous plants** are modified into traps.

**Insectivorous plants** grow in soils poor in **nitrogen** and trap insects to digest and absorb nitrogen compounds. The **pitcher plant** (*Nepenthes*) has a leaf blade modified into a pitcher with a lid and digestive fluid; the **Venus flytrap** (*Dionaea*) has a two-lobed hinged blade with trigger hairs that snaps shut; the sundew (*Drosera*) has sticky tentacles; the bladderwort (*Utricularia*) has small suction bladders. They also photosynthesise, so they trap insects for nitrogen, not for energy.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling a sweet potato a stem (it has no nodes or buds, so it is a root) or a potato a root.
- Giving a modification without its function.
- Calling the spines of *Opuntia* modified stems; they are modified leaves, and the green flattened stem is the phylloclade.
- Telling a compound leaf from a branch by the number of leaflets instead of by the **buds**.
- Writing "alternate" for two leaves at a node; that is opposite phyllotaxy.
- Saying insectivorous plants trap insects for food energy; they need **nitrogen**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a modification, a plant, a function, an adjective for venation or phyllotaxy, a give-a-reason.
- 2- and 3-mark questions: three modifications with plant and function; compound leaf versus branch; parts of a root tip.
- 5-mark questions in parts: a labelled diagram of a root tip or leaf, a table of root or stem modifications, and a reason for a potato being a stem.

questions.stem_md: State the function of (i) the root cap and (ii) the region of maturation of a root.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **root cap** protects the soft **growing tip** as the root pushes through the soil. (ii) In the **region of maturation** cells differentiate, and the **root hairs** formed here **absorb water and minerals** from the soil.

questions.solution_md: Two functions.

questions.stem_md: What are adventitious roots? Give two examples of such roots from different plants.

answer.model_answer_md: **Adventitious roots** arise from parts of the plant **other than the radicle**, such as the stem or a leaf. Examples are the **prop roots of banyan** and the **roots of grass** growing from the nodes (or the roots from the leaf of *Bryophyllum*).

questions.solution_md: Definition and two examples.

questions.stem_md: Explain why mangrove trees growing in tidal mud develop pneumatophores.

answer.model_answer_md: The **waterlogged mud** contains **very little oxygen**, so ordinary roots cannot respire. **Pneumatophores** grow **upward above the mud** and have **pores** through which **air enters** and reaches the roots.

questions.solution_md: Little oxygen; pores for air.

questions.stem_md: Name three kinds of storage roots, giving one plant for each and the shape that identifies it.

answer.model_answer_md:

2. **Conical**: **carrot**, broad at the top and tapering gradually towards the base.
3. **Napiform**: **turnip**, nearly spherical at the top and tapering abruptly below. (Sweet potato is **tuberous**, with no definite shape.)

questions.solution_md: Three types with plants and shapes.

questions.stem_md: A gardener lifts a seedling from a nursery bed with a tight pull and replants it. It wilts for several days and then recovers. Explain what was damaged and how it recovered.

answer.model_answer_md: The pull tore off many **root hairs** of the **region of maturation**, which **absorb water and minerals**, so the plant **wilted**. The **meristematic region** continued to divide and the cells in the **region of elongation** lengthened, so the root grew and produced **new root hairs**, and the plant recovered.

questions.solution_md: Root hairs lost; new growth.

answer.model_answer_md: A **tuber** is a **swollen, rounded** underground stem with **eyes** on the surface, as in **potato**. A **rhizome** is a **horizontal, elongated** underground stem with distinct **nodes and scale leaves**, as in **ginger**.

questions.stem_md: How does a sucker differ from a runner? Give a plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md: A **runner** grows **horizontally along the soil surface** and roots at its nodes, as in **grass**. A **sucker** arises from a **lateral underground node**, grows obliquely upward and gives a new plant, as in **mint**.

questions.solution_md: Runner vs sucker.

questions.stem_md: Why is the green, flat part of Opuntia a stem and not a leaf? State one function it performs.

answer.model_answer_md: It bears **nodes with buds and spines** (the real leaves are modified into **spines**), so it is a **stem**, a **phylloclade**. It carries out **photosynthesis** because the true leaves are reduced, and it also **stores water**.

questions.stem_md: Name three underground stem modifications, giving a plant and a function for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Tuber**: **potato**, a swollen underground stem that stores food and propagates through its eyes, which are axillary buds.
2. **Rhizome**: **ginger** or turmeric, a horizontal stem with nodes and scale leaves that stores food and helps the plant to survive an unfavourable season (perennation).
3. **Corm**: **colocasia**, a short, thick, vertical stem with scale leaves that stores food.

questions.solution_md: Three modifications with plants and functions.

questions.stem_md: Name three sub-aerial stem modifications and state their common function.

answer.model_answer_md: **Runner** (grass), **stolon** (strawberry) and **sucker** (mint), and also **offset** (water hyacinth), are **sub-aerial stems**. They lie along or just below the soil surface and their common function is **vegetative propagation**: their nodes root and give rise to new plants, so that a single plant can spread quickly over a wide area without seeds.

questions.solution_md: Three examples and function.

answer.model_answer_md: The **potato** has **eyes**, which are **axillary buds** on nodes with scale-leaf scars, and a terminal bud; it is a **stem**. The **sweet potato** has **no nodes, internodes or buds**, so it is a **root**. Only the potato sprouts shoots from the regular buds, and the sweet potato forms adventitious shoots.

questions.solution_md: Parallel venation is typical of monocots — option (d).

questions.solution_md: Opposite leaves: 6 × 2 = 12, each with 7 leaflets: 12 × 7 = 84. Whorled simple leaves: 4 × 6 = 24. Total = 84 + 24 = 108.

questions.solution_md: False. A bud is present in the axil of the compound leaf (at the base of its petiole) but not in the axils of the leaflets.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish reticulate venation from parallel venation, naming the plant group in which each is typical.

answer.model_answer_md: In **reticulate venation** the veins form a **network** and the midrib gives branching veins; it is typical of **dicots**. In **parallel venation** the veins run **side by side** from base to tip; it is typical of **monocots**.

questions.solution_md: Two types with groups.

questions.stem_md: What are stipules? How does the leaf base of a grass differ from that of a dicot leaf?

answer.model_answer_md: **Stipules** are small **lateral outgrowths of the leaf base**, found in many dicot leaves. The leaf base of a **grass** expands into a **sheath** that clasps the stem, whereas in many dicots it is small and bears stipules.

questions.solution_md: Stipules and sheath.

questions.stem_md: State two points that distinguish a pinnate compound leaf from a branch bearing simple leaves.

answer.model_answer_md: A **compound leaf** has a **bud only in the axil of its petiole** and **no terminal bud** on its rachis, and the **leaflets have no buds** in their axils. A **branch** has a **terminal bud** and a **bud in the axil of every leaf**.

questions.solution_md: Terminal bud and axillary buds.

marking_scheme.step: Axillary buds in leaflets absent vs in leaves present

questions.stem_md: Name the three parts of a typical dicot leaf and state one function of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **leaf base** attaches the leaf to the stem and may bear **stipules**. The **petiole** holds the **lamina** to the light and lets it move. The **lamina** (blade) is the flat green part that carries out **photosynthesis** and has a **midrib** and **veins** that conduct water and food.

questions.solution_md: Three parts and functions.

questions.stem_md: Define phyllotaxy and describe its three types, giving one plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Phyllotaxy** is the **arrangement of leaves on a stem**. In **alternate** phyllotaxy one leaf arises at each node (China rose, mustard); in **opposite** phyllotaxy two leaves arise at each node (*Calotropis*, guava); in **whorled** phyllotaxy more than two leaves arise at a node (*Alstonia*).

questions.solution_md: Definition and three types.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a pinnate compound leaf from a palmate compound leaf, naming one plant for each, and say how a compound leaf differs from a branch.

answer.model_answer_md: In a **pinnate** compound leaf the leaflets lie along a common axis, the **rachis** (neem). In a **palmate** compound leaf they all arise from the **tip of the petiole** (silk cotton). A compound leaf has an **axillary bud at its base** and **no terminal bud**, whereas a **branch** has a terminal bud and buds in the axils of its leaves.

questions.solution_md: Pinnate vs palmate; compound leaf vs branch.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a simple dicot leaf attached to a stem, naming the leaf base, petiole, lamina, midrib and stipules. [3]
(b) What type of venation does it show? [1]
(c) Name one feature by which a compound leaf is told from a branch. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **stem** with a node; the **leaf base** with a pair of **stipules**, the **petiole**, and the **lamina** with its **midrib** and veins, all labelled.

(b) **Reticulate** venation, as is typical of dicots.

(c) A compound leaf has **no terminal bud** on its rachis and **no buds in the axils of its leaflets**.

questions.solution_md: Diagram; reticulate; bud test.

questions.solution_md: Adventitious buds on the leaf margin of Bryophyllum give new plants — option (a).

options.text_md: fleshy scale leaves that store food

questions.solution_md: The layers of a bulb are fleshy scale leaves storing food — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A pitcher plant grows on soil that is very poor in nitrogen. Its pitcher is a modified

options.text_md: leaf blade, which traps insects to obtain nitrogen

questions.solution_md: The pitcher of Nepenthes is a modified leaf that traps and digests insects for nitrogen — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The Venus flytrap snaps its two lobes shut when an insect touches its trigger hairs. These lobes are

options.text_md: the two halves of a modified leaf blade

questions.solution_md: The hinged trap of Dionaea is a modified leaf blade — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a garden pea the upper leaflets are coiled and cling to a support. These coils are

options.text_md: leaf tendrils, modified leaflets for climbing

questions.solution_md: Modified leaflets that coil for support are leaf tendrils — option (d).

**Assertion (A):** The tendrils of a pea plant are modified leaflets.

**Reason (R):** Tendrils of all plants are modified roots.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Insectivorous plants cannot make their own food.

**Reason (R):** They trap insects because their soil is rich in nitrogen.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false: they photosynthesise and trap insects because the soil is poor in nitrogen — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give a reason: Pitcher plants grow in marshy soil and still trap insects.

answer.model_answer_md: The soil is **poor in nitrogen**, and the insects supply **nitrogen compounds**.

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen from insects.

questions.stem_md: How does Bryophyllum reproduce from its leaves? Name the type of leaf modification.

answer.model_answer_md: In **Bryophyllum** **adventitious buds** form in the **notches of the leaf margin**. They develop into **small plantlets**, which fall to the soil and grow into new plants. This is a leaf modification for **reproduction**.

questions.solution_md: Buds in notches; reproduction.

marking_scheme.step: Plantlets from buds in the notches

questions.stem_md: A leaf tendril and a stem tendril both help in climbing. How can you tell them apart?

answer.model_answer_md: A **stem tendril** arises from an **axillary bud** (as in grapevine), so it occupies the position of a branch. A **leaf tendril** is a **modified leaf or leaflet** (as in pea) and has **no axillary bud of its own**; it arises from the leaf itself.

questions.solution_md: Origin.

marking_scheme.step: Leaf tendril is a leaf or leaflet, no bud

questions.stem_md: Give three modifications of leaves with a function and a plant for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Tendrils** for **support** and climbing, as in the **pea**.
2. **Spines** for **protection** (and less water loss), as in **Opuntia**.
3. **Fleshy scale leaves** for **storage** of food and water, as in the **onion bulb**. (Buds on the margin of *Bryophyllum* serve for reproduction.)

questions.solution_md: Three modifications with function and plant.

marking_scheme.step: Fleshy leaves with function and plant

questions.stem_md: Why do some green plants trap insects? Describe how a pitcher plant or a Venus flytrap does so.

answer.model_answer_md: They grow on soils **poor in nitrogen** and use insects as a source of **nitrogen**. In the **pitcher plant** the **leaf blade forms a pitcher with a lid** and digestive fluid into which insects slip and are **digested**. In the **Venus flytrap** the **two lobes of the blade** **snap shut** when **trigger hairs** are touched.

questions.solution_md: Nitrogen; trap.

questions.stem_md: In Opuntia the leaves are spines, but the plant is green and makes its own food. Explain how, with the name of the part involved.

answer.model_answer_md: The **leaves are reduced to spines**, which **protect** the plant and lose little water. The **stem is flat, green and fleshy**, a **phylloclade**, which contains **chlorophyll** and carries out **photosynthesis**, and also **stores water** in the desert, where water is scarce and a large leaf surface would lose too much of it.

questions.solution_md: Spines; phylloclade does photosynthesis.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name three leaf modifications for support, storage and reproduction, with a plant for each. [3]
(b) What do insectivorous plants obtain from the insects they trap and why do they need it? [1]
(c) Name two insectivorous plants. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Support:** leaf tendrils of **pea**. **Storage:** fleshy scale leaves of **onion**. **Reproduction:** buds in the notches of the leaf margin of **Bryophyllum**.

(b) They obtain **nitrogen compounds**, needed because their soil is **poor in nitrogen**.

(c) **Nepenthes** (pitcher plant) and **Dionaea** (Venus flytrap); also **Drosera** and **Utricularia**.

questions.solution_md: Three modifications; nitrogen; two plants.

A student collected five plant parts from a kitchen garden.

| Specimen | Observations |
|---|---|
| P | Thick, cone-shaped, orange, no nodes; leaves grow from its top |
| Q | Underground, horizontal, jointed, with scale leaves and buds |
| R | Green, flat, fleshy pad with small spines |
| S | Coiled thread arising in a leaf axil of a climbing vine |
| T | Several leaves around each node of a woody twig |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) P, conical

**(b)** (b) Q and S

**(c)** (i) T shows **whorled phyllotaxy**, with **more than two leaves at a node**, as in *Alstonia*.

**OR** (ii) R is a **phylloclade**, a modified **stem**, and its **spines** are **modified leaves**, as in *Opuntia*.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** P has no nodes and a conical shape, like a carrot — option (a).

**(b)** Q is a rhizome and S, a tendril from an axillary position, is a stem tendril — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Whorled; Alstonia.

(ii) Phylloclade; leaf spines.
